claim: AAV-Gfap-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry was selectively expressed in GFAP-expressing glia in the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of adult mice.
source: This was achieved by stereotaxic injection in ARC with an adeno-associated virus (AAV) containing a Gfap promoter-driven gene that encodes the evolved human M3-muscarinic receptor fused to mCherry (hM3D(Gq)-mCherry) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The text describes the experimental method used to achieve selective expression in GFAP-expressing glia, and Figure 1A shows the construct design.

claim: hM3D(Gq)-mCherry was selectively expressed in glia and not in neurons, as evidenced by co-localization with anti-GFAP and anti-S100B but not with anti-NeuN.
source: This was evidenced by the co-localization of mCherry with anti-GFAP (Figure 1C) and anti-S100B (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A: 93.9% of mCherry-expressing cells (n = 401/430 cells in 12 animals) were immunopositive for S100B) but not with anti-neuronal nuclei (NeuN) immunohistochemistry stains (Figure 1D).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data showing co-localization with glial markers and lack of co-localization with neuronal markers, with quantification provided.

claim: 99.1% of GFP-expressing neurons in Npy-hrGFP mice did not express mCherry.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A: 99.1% of GFP-expressing neurons in Npy-hrGFP mice (n = 733/744 neurons in 11 animals) and 99.3% of GFP-expressing neurons in Pomc-EGFP mice (n = 439/448 neurons in 9 animals) did not express mCherry
evidence: Quantitative data from immunohistochemistry showing lack of overlap between mCherry expression and NPY neurons.

claim: 99.3% of GFP-expressing neurons in Pomc-EGFP mice did not express mCherry.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1A: 99.1% of GFP-expressing neurons in Npy-hrGFP mice (n = 733/744 neurons in 11 animals) and 99.3% of GFP-expressing neurons in Pomc-EGFP mice (n = 439/448 neurons in 9 animals) did not express mCherry
evidence: Quantitative data from immunohistochemistry showing lack of overlap between mCherry expression and POMC neurons.

claim: 14.9% of mCherry-expressing cells co-localized with anti-vimentin, a marker for tanycytes.
source: Figure 1—figure supplement 1B: 14.9% of the mCherry-expressing cells co-localized with anti-vimentin, a marker for tanycytes (n = 80/512 mCherry-expressing cells in 4 animals).
evidence: Quantitative immunohistochemistry data showing partial co-localization with tanycyte marker.

claim: In vivo injection of CNO (0.3 mg/kg) induced significantly greater Fos immunoreactivity compared to saline injections in ARC astrocytes.
source: In vivo injections of CNO (0.3 mg/kg) (Koch et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011, 2013; Pei et al., 2014) induced significantly greater Fos immunoreactivity (Palkovits et al., 2007; Ramírez et al., 2015) as compared to saline injections in ARC astrocytes (Figure 1E–F: n = 95 mCherry-expressing astrocytes in 5 animals each for saline and CNO groups, p=0.0114, unpaired t-test, comparing averaged responses across astrocytes in each saline- and CNO-injected animal)
evidence: Statistical comparison of Fos immunoreactivity between CNO and saline conditions with p-value and sample size provided.

claim: CNO injection did not induce significant Fos immunoreactivity in tanycytes.
source: In vivo injections of CNO (0.3 mg/kg) (Koch et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011, 2013; Pei et al., 2014) induced significantly greater Fos immunoreactivity (Palkovits et al., 2007; Ramírez et al., 2015) as compared to saline injections in ARC astrocytes (Figure 1E–F: n = 95 mCherry-expressing astrocytes in 5 animals each for saline and CNO groups, p=0.0114, unpaired t-test, comparing averaged responses across astrocytes in each saline- and CNO-injected animal) but not in tanycytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Reference to figure showing lack of significant Fos response in tanycytes after CNO injection.

claim: CNO application in ARC slices evoked robust Ca2+ responses in hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing astrocytes.
source: CNO, but not saline application in ARC slices (Figure 1G) also evoked robust Ca2+ responses in hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing astrocytes (Figure 1H–I: n = 42 mCherry-expressing astrocytes in 3 animals each for saline and CNO groups, p=5.49E-16, unpaired t-test, comparing averaged responses across astrocytes in the saline- and CNO-injected animals).
evidence: Calcium imaging data with statistical comparison showing significant Ca2+ response to CNO.

claim: Greater complexity of astrocytic processes was observed in CNO-injected animals compared to saline-injected animals.
source: A greater complexity of astrocytic processes was also observed in CNO-injected animals as compared to saline-injected animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: Morphological analysis data showing differences in astrocytic process complexity between conditions.

claim: Greater complexity of astrocytic processes was observed in fasted animals compared to fed animals.
source: A greater complexity of astrocytic processes was also observed in fasted animals as compared to fed animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–J).
evidence: Morphological analysis data showing differences in astrocytic process complexity between fasted and fed conditions.

claim: The average total food intake during days of CNO administration was about three- to four-fold greater than that during baseline, pre-CNO saline and post-CNO saline.
source: Interestingly, the average total food intake during days of CNO administration was about three- to four-fold greater than that during baseline, pre-CNO saline and post-CNO saline (Figure 2B: p<0.0001, n = 11 animals, unpaired t-test comparing total food intake during three days of CNO with that during three days of baseline, three days of pre-CNO saline and four days of post-CNO saline).
evidence: Statistical comparison of food intake across different experimental conditions with p-value and sample size.

claim: The feeding response to CNO was reversible and reproducible across repeated CNO administration in the same animal.
source: This feeding response was reversible and reproducible across repeated CNO administration in the same animal (Figure 2B), suggesting that glial activation may serve as an intrinsic regulatory mechanism of food intake.
evidence: Observation from repeated measurements showing consistent and reversible effects.

claim: CNO administration induced increased food intake within 30 min post injection with peak feeding within 1 hr post injection.
source: The time course revealed increased food intake within 30 min post CNO injection with peak feeding within 1 hr post injection.
evidence: Time course analysis of food intake following CNO injection.

claim: At peak feeding, the food intake was more than 13 times greater than that during saline administration.
source: At peak feeding, the food intake was more than 13 times greater than that during saline administration (Figure 2C).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of food intake at peak feeding between CNO and saline conditions.

claim: The average percentage of time that mice spent at the food chamber following CNO administration was significantly greater than that following saline administration.
source: The average percentage of time that mice spent at the food chamber following CNO administration was significantly greater than that following saline administration in the same mice (Figure 2D: n = 11 animals, ANOVA, Drug: p<0.0001, F(1,20) = 47.8; Time: p<0.0001, F(8,160) = 26.6; Interaction between drug and time: p<0.0001, F(8,160) = 22.7, comparing the population and trial-averaged time spent at food chamber at specific time points between 09:00 and 17:00 during pre-CNO saline and CNO administration).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing time spent at food chamber between CNO and saline conditions.

claim: The frequency of food seeking attempts was significantly greater following CNO administration compared to saline administration.
source: The same was true for the frequency of food seeking attempts (Figure 2E: n = 11 animals, ANOVA, Drug: p=0.003, F(1,20) = 11.4; Time: p<0.0001, F(8,160) = 17.2; Interaction between drug and time: p<0.0001, F(8,160) = 10.1, comparing the population and trial-averaged frequency of attempts at specific time points between 09:00 and 17:00 during pre-CNO saline and CNO administration).
evidence: Statistical analysis of behavioral data comparing frequency of food seeking attempts between CNO and saline conditions.

claim: CNO administration increased the frequency of shorter-duration feeding attempts and increased the maximum duration of the feeding episodes.
source: CNO administration also increased the frequency of shorter-duration feeding attempts and increased the maximum duration of the feeding episodes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Analysis of feeding bout characteristics showing changes in duration patterns.

claim: A trend of increased CNO-induced food intake was observed with increased size of hM3D(Gq)-mCherry expression in the ARC.
source: A trend of increased CNO-induced food intake was observed with increased size of hM3D(Gq)-mCherry expression in the ARC (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Correlation analysis between viral expression size and food intake response.

claim: In mice lacking hM3D(Gq)-mCherry expression in ARC, CNO administration did not increase food intake.
source: In mice lacking hM3D(Gq)-mCherry expression in ARC due to failed viral injection attempts (identified in post hoc analysis) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) as well as mice injected with the control virus AAV-Gfap-mCherry in ARC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5), CNO administration did not increase food intake.
evidence: Control experiments showing no effect of CNO in the absence of hM3D(Gq) expression.

claim: Glial activation did not lead to changes in body weight.
source: Although glial activation resulted in the pronounced feeding response, DREADD activation of glia did not lead to changes in the body weight (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Body weight measurements showing no significant changes despite increased food intake.

claim: The Fos activity of astrocytes in AAV-Gfap-p130PH-mRFP injected animals was significantly lower than that in control animals after fasting.
source: Indeed, the Fos activity of astrocytes in the AAV-Gfap-p130PH-mRFP injected animals was significantly lower than that in the control animals (Figure 3B,C: p130PH: n = 847 mRFP-expressing astrocytes, Control: n = 508 mRFP-expressing astrocytes, 8 animals each, p=0.0264, unpaired t-test, comparing averaged responses across astrocytes in each Gfap-p130PH-mRFP and control animal).
evidence: Statistical comparison of Fos immunoreactivity between experimental and control groups.

claim: The Fos activity of tanycytes was not significantly different between AAV-Gfap-p130PH-mRFP and control animals.
source: The Fos activity of tanycytes, however, was not significantly different between the experimental and control groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant difference in tanycyte Fos activity between groups.

claim: The Fos activity of neurons was significantly lower in AAV-Gfap-p130PH-mRFP injected animals than in control animals.
source: The Fos activity of neurons was significantly lower in experimental than in control animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B), suggesting possible glial-neuronal modulation (see below).
evidence: Statistical comparison of neuronal Fos activity between experimental and control groups.

claim: The population and trial-averaged food intake was significantly lower in Gfap-p130PH-mRFP-injected animals than control animals in the dark phase but not light phase.
source: Interestingly, the population and trial-averaged food intake was significantly lower in Gfap-p130PH-mRFP-injected animals than control animals in the dark phase but not light phase (Figure 4A: n = 8 animals, ANOVA, Drug: p<0.0001, F(1,14) = 30.3; Time: p<0.0001, F(19,266) = 72.9; Interaction between drug and time: p=0.0131, F(19,266) = 1.92).
evidence: Statistical analysis of food intake comparing experimental and control groups across different phases.

claim: The cumulative food intake of Gfap-p130PH-mRFP-injected animals at the 24-hr time point remained significantly lower than control animals.
source: This reduction of food intake during the dark phase was not compensated by an increase in food intake in the light phase as the cumulative food intake of Gfap-p130PH-mRFP-injected animals at the 24-hr time point (19:00) remained significantly lower than control animals (Figure 4B: n = 8 animals, ANOVA, Drug: p<0.0001, F(1,14) = 44.7; Time: p<0.0001, F(19,266) = 1091; Interaction between drug and time: p<0.0001, F(19,266) = 16.4).
evidence: Statistical analysis of cumulative food intake over 24 hours.

claim: CNO activation of hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing ARC glia depolarized and/or increased the firing rate of AgRP/NPY neurons.
source: Interestingly, CNO activation of the hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing ARC glia depolarized and/or increased the firing rate of AgRP/NPY neurons (Figure 5B,C: n = 15 neurons in 15 slices from 9 animals, p<0.0001, unpaired t-test, comparing CNO-induced responses with null responses; averaged resting membrane potential: −52.2 ± 2.65 mV [van den Top et al., 2004]).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing depolarization and increased firing in response to CNO.

claim: In POMC neurons, CNO did not induce a significant response at a population level.
source: In POMC neurons, CNO did not induce a significant response at a population level (Figure 5B,C: n = 14 neurons in 14 slices in 6 animals, p=0.370; unpaired t-test, comparing CNO-induced responses with null responses; averaged resting membrane potential: - 44.1 ± 2.09 mV [Cowley et al., 2001]).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing no significant population response in POMC neurons.

claim: Greater Fos immunoreactivity was observed after CNO injection compared to saline injection in NPY neurons.
source: Indeed, greater Fos immunoreactivity was observed after CNO injection as compared to saline injection in NPY but not POMC neurons (Figure 5D–E,F: n = 5 Npy-hrGFP animals each for CNO and saline injections, p=0.0428, unpaired t-test, comparing CNO and saline induced responses; n = 5 and n = 6 Pomc-EGFP animals for CNO and saline injections respectively, p=0.736, unpaired t-test, comparing CNO and saline induced responses).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data comparing Fos expression in NPY neurons between CNO and saline conditions.

claim: No significant difference in Fos immunoreactivity was observed after CNO injection compared to saline injection in POMC neurons.
source: Indeed, greater Fos immunoreactivity was observed after CNO injection as compared to saline injection in NPY but not POMC neurons (Figure 5D–E,F: n = 5 Npy-hrGFP animals each for CNO and saline injections, p=0.0428, unpaired t-test, comparing CNO and saline induced responses; n = 5 and n = 6 Pomc-EGFP animals for CNO and saline injections respectively, p=0.736, unpaired t-test, comparing CNO and saline induced responses).
evidence: Immunohistochemistry data showing no significant difference in Fos expression in POMC neurons between CNO and saline conditions.

claim: BAPTA chelation of Ca2+ in hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing ARC astrocytes blocked the CNO-evoked depolarization in NPY neurons.
source: Indeed, BAPTA chelation of Ca2+ in hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-expressing ARC astrocytes blocked the CNO-evoked depolarization in NPY neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–D: Control: n = 15 neurons in 15 slices in 9 animals, BAPTA: n = 5 neurons (patched after BAPTA dialysis of astrocyte syncytium) in 5 slices in 3 animals, p=0.0050, unpaired t-test, comparing responses in the absence and presence of BAPTA dialysis).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings with astrocytic Ca2+ chelation showing blockade of neuronal response.

claim: CNO evoked an increase in the frequency but not amplitude of sIPSCs in POMC neurons.
source: Indeed, CNO evoked an increase in the frequency (but not amplitude) of sIPSCs in POMC neurons (Figure 6A top, 6B: n = 7 neurons in 7 slices in 3 animals, Amplitude: p=0.324; Frequency: p=0.0078, paired t-test, comparing normalized responses before and after CNO application).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings of inhibitory postsynaptic currents showing increased frequency.

claim: CNO evoked strong depolarization in POMC neurons when patched in the presence of GABA receptor blockers.
source: Interestingly, CNO evoked strong depolarization in POMC neurons when patched in the presence of GABAR blockers (Figure 6A bottom, Figure 6C: Control: n = 14 neurons in 14 slices in 6 animals, GABAR blockers: n = 7 neurons in 7 slices in 5 animals, p=0.0046, unpaired t-test, comparing responses between in the absence and presence of GABAR blockers).
evidence: Electrophysiological recordings showing depolarization when inhibition is blocked.

claim: The average total food intake during days of CNO administration was not significantly different from that during saline administration in animals with simultaneous glial activation and AgRP/NPY neuronal inactivation.
source: The average total food intake (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D) as well as population and trial-averaged time course of food intake (Figure 5—figure supplement 2E) during days of CNO administration were not significantly different from those during saline administration.
evidence: Food intake measurements showing no significant difference when AgRP/NPY neurons are inactivated during glial activation.

claim: ARC glial activation enables increase in food intake via AgRP/NPY neurons.
source: Our work shows that ARC glial activation enables increase in food intake via AgRP/NPY neurons.
evidence: Summary statement based on the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: ARC glial activation facilitates both AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons.
source: Interestingly, ARC glial activation facilitates both AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons.
evidence: Summary statement based on electrophysiological findings.

claim: The responses in POMC neurons are shaped by an inhibitory input, possibly due to activation of the AgRP/NPY neuron-POMC neuron inhibitory pathway.
source: Unlike AgRP/NPY neurons, however, the responses in POMC neurons are further shaped by an inhibitory input, possibly due to activation of the AgRP/NPY neuron-POMC neuron inhibitory pathway (Atasoy et al., 2012).
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings with reference to known circuit connectivity.

claim: Glial cells interact with distinct neuronal subtypes non-specifically but can confer neuronal subtype-specific modulation through direct modulation of distinct neuronal circuits.
source: Our findings show that although glial cells interact with distinct neuronal subtypes non-specifically, it can confer neuronal subtype-specific modulation through direct modulation of distinct neuronal circuits.
evidence: Interpretation and generalization of the experimental findings.

claim: The lack of astrocyte-neuronal subtype wiring suggests that glial activation may modulate other neuronal subtypes within the ARC.
source: The lack of astrocyte-neuronal subtype wiring also suggests that glial activation may modulate other neuronal subtypes within the ARC.
evidence: Inference based on the non-specific nature of glial-neuronal interactions observed.

claim: Glial modulation of energy expenditure-promoting neurons in ARC may prevent expected body weight gains during AgRP/NPY neuronal activation.
source: This thus opens the possibility of glial modulation of energy expenditure-promoting neurons in ARC e.g. GABAergic RIP-Cre neurons which do not overlap with the POMC and AgRP/NPY neuronal population (Kong et al., 2012) and can potentially prevent the expected body weight gains during AgRP/NPY neuronal activation (Krashes et al., 2011). This may explain the absence of weight changes during ARC glial modulation observed in our study (Figure 2—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Speculation about mechanism explaining observed lack of body weight changes, with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Possible mechanisms underlying non-specific glial activation-stimulation of neurons include astrocytic release of glutamate or D-serine gliotransmitters.
source: There are a few possible mechanisms that may underlie the non-specific, glial activation-stimulation of AgRP neurons and POMC neurons. These include: (1) astrocytic release of glutamate or D-serine gliotransmitters (Halassa et al., 2007; Haydon and Carmignoto, 2006; Parpura and Zorec, 2010; Scofield et al., 2015; Volterra and Meldolesi, 2005);
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Possible mechanisms underlying non-specific glial activation-stimulation of neurons include regulation of extracellular transmitters or extracellular potassium possibly through changes in the activity of transporters in the astrocyte membrane.
source: (2) regulation of extracellular transmitters (Pannasch et al., 2014) or extracellular potassium (Wang et al., 2012) possibly through changes in the activity of transporters in the astrocyte membrane (Bazargani and Attwell, 2016).
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Under physiological conditions, glial activation may occur via neuronal-glial interactions, possibly evoked by active AgRP/NPY neurons in the presence of a strong drive to feed.
source: Under physiological conditions, glial activation may occur via neuronal-glial interactions (Allen and Barres, 2009; Bazargani and Attwell, 2016; Fields and Burnstock, 2006; Lalo et al., 2006), possibly evoked by active AgRP/NPY neurons in the presence of a strong drive to feed (Chen et al., 2015; Mandelblat-Cerf et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculation about physiological mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Bidirectional communication between glia and neurons modulates feeding.
source: This, together with the strong glial-neuronal interactions observed in our work (Figure 5A–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1G, Figure 3B–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) suggest modulation of feeding by bidirectional communication (Allen and Barres, 2009) between glia and neurons.
evidence: Inference based on experimental observations with citation to relevant concept.

claim: Direct glial modulation by orexigenic molecules such as ghrelin via astrocytic ghrelin receptors may be a possible mechanism to glial activation.
source: Direct glial modulation by orexigenic molecules (Murphy and Bloom, 2006) such as ghrelin via astrocytic ghrelin receptors (García-Cáceres et al., 2014) may also be a possible mechanism to glial activation.
evidence: Speculation about possible mechanisms with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The Gq-DREADD technology mimics acute activation of astrocytic GPCRs that triggers Ca2+ activation.
source: The Gq-DREADD technology mimics acute activation of astrocytic GPCRs that triggers Ca2+ activation (Agulhon et al., 2013, 2008)
evidence: Description of the technology with citations to relevant literature.

claim: The p130PH technology enables disruption of the endogenous PLC/IP3 glial Ca2+ signaling during physiological feeding states.
source: while the p130PH technology enables disruption of the endogenous PLC/IP3 glial Ca2+ signaling (Li et al., 2013; Xie et al., 2015, 2010) during physiological feeding states.
evidence: Description of the technology with citations to relevant literature.

claim: It is unclear whether Gi-DREADD can affect glial activity or glial Ca2+ signaling pathways as glial cells are electrically non-excitable and do not fire action potentials.
source: Although the Gi-DREADD technology has been shown to inhibit neuronal firing via induction of hyperpolarization and inhibition of presynaptic neurotransmitter release (Roth, 2016), it is unclear whether Gi-DREADD can affect glial activity or glial Ca2+ signaling pathways as these cells are electrically non-excitable and do not fire action potentials.
evidence: Discussion of limitations of a technology based on known properties of glial cells.

claim: Existing work that activated Gi-coupled GPCR pathways in glia do not reveal any blockade of both astrocytic activity and astrocyte-neuronal modulation.
source: In addition, existing work that activated Gi-coupled GPCR pathways in glia do not reveal any blockade of both astrocytic activity and astrocyte-neuronal modulation (Agulhon et al., 2012).
evidence: Citation to existing literature showing lack of effect.

claim: Glial Gi-DREADD activation did not have any effect on feeding.
source: Indeed, we did not observe any effect of glial Gi-DREADD activation on feeding (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Experimental data showing no effect of Gi-DREADD on feeding.

claim: Previous work has provided evidence that supports the role for astrocytes in feeding through chronic modification of feeding by synaptic remodeling during conditional deletion of astrocytic leptin receptors.
source: Previous work has provided evidence that support the role for astrocytes in feeding. This includes experiments showing chronic modification of feeding by synaptic remodeling (Horvath et al., 2010) during conditional deletion of astrocytic leptin receptors (Kim et al., 2014) (see also Jayaram et al., 2013)
evidence: Summary of previous literature with citations.

claim: Previous work has observed reactive gliosis and activation of astrocytic inflammatory signaling pathways after feeding of high fat diet.
source: as well as observation of reactive gliosis (Horvath et al., 2010) and activation of astrocytic inflammatory signaling pathways after feeding of high fat diet (Buckman et al., 2015).
evidence: Summary of previous literature with citations.

claim: Previous studies do not address whether direct glial-activation can evoke acute changes in feeding.
source: These studies however do not address the question of whether direct glial-activation can evoke acute changes in feeding.
evidence: Critical assessment of gaps in previous literature.

claim: The behavioral changes in feeding in previous studies cannot be solely isolated to the hypothalamus due to body-wide deletion of leptin receptors in GFAP-expressing cells.
source: The behavioral changes in feeding in these studies also cannot be solely isolated to the hypothalamus due to body-wide deletion of leptin receptors in GFAP-expressing cells (expression of GFAP (Apte et al., 1998; Buniatian et al., 1998; Nolte et al., 2001) and leptin receptors (Bjørbaek and Kahn, 2004; Gautron and Elmquist, 2011) occur in both the central nervous system and periphery).
evidence: Critical assessment of limitations in previous studies with citations to relevant literature.

claim: This work demonstrates a causal relationship between arcuate glia and acute as well as chronic modulation of food intake.
source: Our work directly addresses these gaps in knowledge by demonstrating a causal relationship between arcuate glia and acute as well as chronic modulation of food intake.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: This work provides mechanistic evidence to explain how glial activation can differentially modulate AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons through direct modulation of distinct neuronal pathways.
source: We also further provide mechanistic evidence to explain how glial activation can differentially modulate AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons through direct modulation of distinct neuronal pathways
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: This work demonstrates the necessity of active AgRP/NPY neurons in mediating the glial activation-induced feeding.
source: and demonstrate the necessity of active AgRP/NPY neurons in mediating the glial activation-induced feeding.
evidence: Summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: A previous study investigating glial regulation of feeding using the CNO-DREADD system reported distinct conclusions from this study.
source: A previous study (Yang et al., 2015) investigating glial regulation of feeding by using the CNO-DREADD system reported distinct conclusions from our study.
evidence: Comparison with previous literature.

claim: The differences with a previous study are attributed to the use of different CNO doses, with a high CNO dose (5 mg/kg) inducing non-specific inhibition in feeding.
source: We attribute the differences to the use of different CNO doses and show that a high CNO dose (5 mg/kg) used in that study (Yang et al., 2015) can in fact induce non-specific inhibition in feeding (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D), possibly due to CNO-induced ataxia (Sigma-Aldrich's toxicological studies [Sigma-Aldrich, 2016]).
evidence: Experimental data and citation to toxicological information explaining discrepancy with previous study.

claim: This work, together with previous findings, demonstrates a critical role of glia in the regulation of feeding and establishes ARC as an important site of glial-mediated regulation.
source: Our work, together with previous findings, collectively demonstrates a critical role of glia in the regulation of feeding and further establishes ARC as an important site of glial-mediated regulation.
evidence: Summary statement integrating current findings with previous literature.

claim: These findings imply a possible causal link between increased ARC glial Ca2+ during astrogliosis and hyperphagia during ARC inflammation.
source: These findings also imply a possible causal link between increased ARC glial Ca2+ during astrogliosis (Kanemaru et al., 2013) and hyperphagia during ARC inflammation (Dorfman and Thaler, 2015).
evidence: Speculation about broader implications with citations to relevant literature.

claim: Future work may reveal glia as a possible target of therapeutic intervention.
source: Future work in this area may reveal glia as a possible target of therapeutic intervention.
evidence: Speculation about future directions and potential applications.

claim: The hM3D(Gq) couples to the Gq protein-mediated signaling to activate glia upon binding of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO).
source: The hM3D(Gq) couples to the Gq protein-mediated signaling to activate glia upon binding of clozapine-N-oxide (CNO).
evidence: Description of the mechanism of action of the DREADD system.

claim: CNO is an exclusively specific ligand of DREADD and is inert when used at low concentrations.
source: CNO is an exclusively specific ligand of DREADD (Agulhon et al., 2013) and is inert when used at low concentrations (see CNO dose experiments in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Statement about CNO specificity with citation and reference to experimental data.

claim: The hM3D(Gq)-mCherry glial population comprised both astrocytes and tanycytes that line the third ventricle.
source: The hM3D(Gq)-mCherry glial population comprised both astrocytes and tanycytes that line the third ventricle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B: 14.9% of the mCherry-expressing cells co-localized with anti-vimentin, a marker for tanycytes (n = 80/512 mCherry-expressing cells in 4 animals).
evidence: Characterization of cell types expressing the construct with quantification.

claim: Activation of hM3D(Gq)-mCherry in astrocytes can induce both the functional and morphological changes observed during physiological activation of astrocytes after fasting.
source: These data suggest that activation of hM3D(Gq)-mCherry in astrocytes can induce both the functional and morphological changes observed during physiological activation of astrocytes after fasting.
evidence: Inference based on comparison of DREADD activation effects with physiological fasting effects.

claim: The CNO dose was selected to be 0.3 mg/kg for all experiments, as concentration experiments revealed non-specific inhibition of food intake at high but not low CNO concentration.
source: The CNO dose was selected to be 0.3 mg/kg (Koch et al., 2015; Krashes et al., 2011, 2013; Pei et al., 2014) for all experiments, as concentration experiments in control mice with low (0.3 mg/kg) and high (5 mg/kg) (Yang et al., 2015) CNO concentrations revealed non-specific inhibition of food intake at high but not low CNO concentration (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: Justification for dose selection based on experimental data and citations.

claim: The feeding response to glial activation was reversible and reproducible, suggesting that glial activation may serve as an intrinsic regulatory mechanism of food intake.
source: This feeding response was reversible and reproducible across repeated CNO administration in the same animal (Figure 2B), suggesting that glial activation may serve as an intrinsic regulatory mechanism of food intake.
evidence: Inference based on the reversible and reproducible nature of the observed effect.

claim: CNO administration evoked increased food intake within 3 hr post CNO application in the dark phase when majority of food intake occurs.
source: It is worth mentioning that CNO administration evoked increased food intake within 3 hr post CNO application in the dark phase when majority of food intake occurs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: Experimental data showing effect during dark phase.

claim: The total food intake in the 8 hr of dark phase was not significantly different between CNO and saline application.
source: The total food intake in the 8 hr of dark phase was however not significantly different between CNO and saline application (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Experimental data showing no overall difference in dark phase total food intake.

claim: The lack of difference in total dark phase food intake may be due to a ceiling effect in the drive to feed when glia may already be activated at night.
source: This may be due to a ceiling effect in the drive to feed when glia may already be activated at night (see section below).
evidence: Speculation about mechanism explaining the observation.

claim: Glial expression of the p130PH construct was previously shown to disrupt the Ca2+ signaling in astrocytes in vivo by acting as a mobile cytosolic IP3 buffer to inhibit release of Ca2+ from internal stores.
source: Glial expression of the p130PH construct was previously shown to disrupt the Ca2+  signaling in astrocytes in vivo by acting as a mobile cytosolic IP3 buffer to inhibit release of Ca2+ from internal stores (Xie et al., 2010).
evidence: Citation to previous work describing the mechanism of the p130PH construct.

claim: No significant difference in body weight was observed between Gfap-p130PH-mRFP-injected animals and control animals.

claim: Astrocytes are integral components of brain circuits linked to specific brain functions and are capable of modulating neuronal responses.
source: There is emerging evidence that astrocytes are integral components of brain circuits linked to specific brain functions and are capable of modulating neuronal responses (Eroglu and Barres, 2010; Halassa and Haydon, 2010).
evidence: Statement of established knowledge with citations.

claim: Astrocytic Ca2+ activation contributes to NPY neuronal facilitation.

claim: Direct and acute activation of ARC glia facilitates the activity of AgRP/NPY but not POMC neurons.
source: Collectively, these observations show that direct and acute activation of ARC glia facilitates the activity of AgRP/NPY but not POMC neurons.
evidence: Summary of electrophysiological and immunohistochemistry findings.

claim: Astrocytic activation facilitates both AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons indiscriminately, but the presence of a strong inhibitory input leads to no net response in POMC neurons.
source: These data support our hypothesis that astrocytic activation facilitates both AgRP/NPY and POMC neurons indiscriminately. Unlike AgRP/NPY neurons, however, the presence of a strong inhibitory input, possibly due to the activation of AgRP/NPY-POMC inhibitory connection (Atasoy et al., 2012) during glial activation, can further shape the net responses of POMC neurons.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings with citation to known circuit connectivity.

claim: ARC glial activation indiscriminately facilitates both AgRP/NPY neurons and POMC neurons but the presence of an inhibitory input leads to no net response in POMC neurons, providing a mechanistic understanding of the glial activation-induced increase in feeding.
source: Our data thus suggest that ARC glial activation indiscriminately facilitates both AgRP/NPY neurons and POMC neurons but the presence of an inhibitory input leads to no net response in POMC neurons, thereby providing a mechanistic understanding of the glial activation-induced increase in feeding.
evidence: Summary statement integrating multiple experimental findings into a mechanistic model.

claim: AgRP/NPY activation is necessary for glial activation-induced increase in feeding.
source: This finding that AgRP/NPY activation is required to mediate the glial activation-induced increase in feeding further establishes the crucial role of the ARC glia-AgRP/NPY circuit in the regulation of energy balance.
evidence: Conclusion based on experiments with simultaneous glial activation and AgRP/NPY neuronal inactivation.

claim: This may be a common mechanism to explain the glial-neuronal subtype specific modulation observed in other brain regions.

evidence: Speculation about generalizability with citation.
